steps.body: Multiples of a unit fraction are the clearest case: 4 × 1/6 is simply four sixth-pieces, so the answer is 4/6.

commonFractions.feedback: 1/6 is a single piece; four of them were collected.
4/12 shrank the pieces. Collecting sixths leaves you holding sixths.

predict.reveal: Four sixth-pieces are four sixths. Collecting pieces never makes them smaller.

cml.actionGoal: Collect equal groups of a fraction and watch only the COUNT of pieces change for g4x unit multiples.
invariants: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number collects groups of identical pieces: the denominator names the piece size and holds still, while the numerator counts every piece gathered, which is what keeps g4x unit multiples a counting problem.
misconceptions: Scaling the denominator along with the numerator, adding the whole number to the numerator, or assuming a product cannot pass one whole.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the denominator DID change when you collected groups, what would happen to the size of each piece?

widget.prompt: Compute 2 × 1/3 as ?/3. What is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is the DENOMINATOR — it names the piece size and never changes when you collect pieces.
Adding the two numbers mixes a count of pieces with a piece size; only the count grows.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count the same-size pieces the groups collect; the denominator never changes.

options.feedback: Correct — three equal groups of 2/5, which is exactly what repeated addition of the same fraction means.
That multiplies the fractions together, which shrinks them; the story repeats one fraction three times.
Adding 3 counts three wholes, not three copies of 2/5.
That scaled the denominator too. Collecting three groups of 2/5 keeps fifths and gives 6/5.
